name: Primality Test
description: Returns 1 if n is a prime number and 0 otherwise. The test is exact (deterministic Miller–Rabin) for every integer the app can hold.
notes: Negative numbers, 0 and 1 are not prime. 2147483647 = 2^31 − 1 is a Mersenne prime.

name: Next Prime
description: Gives the smallest prime strictly greater than n.
notes: The next prime after one million is 1,000,003.

name: Previous Prime
description: Gives the largest prime strictly smaller than n.
notes: n must be at least 3. The largest prime below one million is 999,983.

name: Prime-Counting Function π(x)
description: Counts the primes less than or equal to x exactly, using the Lucy–Hedgehog (Legendre-type) method.
notes: Exact for x up to 10^11. π(10^6) = 78,498.

name: n-th Prime
description: Gives the n-th prime number p_n, counting 2 as the first.
notes: Available for n up to 2,000,000. The 10,000th prime is 104,729.

name: Prime Gap After n
description: Gives the gap between the first prime above n and the prime just before it — the length of the prime gap that n falls in or ends.
notes: Around 1327 lies the first gap of length 34 (1327 to 1361).

name: Twin Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when p and p + 2 are both prime, so that (p, p + 2) is a twin-prime pair.
notes: Whether infinitely many twin primes exist is the open twin prime conjecture.

name: Cousin Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when p and p + 4 are both prime (a cousin-prime pair).

name: Sexy Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when p and p + 6 are both prime (a "sexy" prime pair, from the Latin sex = six).

name: Prime Triplet Test
description: Returns 1 when p, p + 6 and either p + 2 or p + 4 are all prime — the two admissible forms of a prime triplet.

name: Prime Quadruplet Test
description: Returns 1 when p, p + 2, p + 6 and p + 8 are all prime, the densest possible cluster of four primes.

name: Sophie Germain Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when p is prime and 2p + 1 is also prime; p is then a Sophie Germain prime and 2p + 1 a safe prime.
notes: These primes appear in Sophie Germain's work on Fermat's Last Theorem and in cryptography (safe-prime groups).

name: Safe Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when p is prime and (p − 1)/2 is also prime, which makes p a safe prime.
notes: Safe primes give multiplicative groups with a large prime-order subgroup, used in Diffie–Hellman key exchange.

name: Chen Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when p is prime and p + 2 is either prime or a product of two primes (a Chen prime).
notes: Chen Jingrun proved in 1973 that there are infinitely many such primes.

name: Balanced Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when the prime p is the average of the primes just before and after it.

name: Emirp Test
description: Returns 1 when n is prime, its digits reversed form a different prime ("emirp" is "prime" spelled backwards).
notes: Palindromic primes are excluded. 107 and 701 are both prime.

name: Palindromic Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when n is prime and reads the same forwards and backwards.
notes: Apart from 11, every palindromic prime has an odd number of digits, because even-length palindromes are divisible by 11.

name: Mersenne Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when the Mersenne number 2^p − 1 is prime.
notes: p must itself be prime for 2^p − 1 to be prime, but that is not enough (2^11 − 1 = 2047 = 23 × 89). Exact for p up to 53.

name: Perfect Number from a Mersenne Prime
description: Builds the even perfect number 2^(p−1)(2^p − 1) from a Mersenne prime 2^p − 1 (Euclid–Euler theorem).
notes: Every even perfect number has this form. p = 2, 3, 5, 7 give 6, 28, 496, 8128.

name: Wilson's Theorem Test
description: Returns 1 when (n − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod n), which by Wilson's theorem happens exactly when n is prime.
notes: An elegant characterisation of primes, though slower than other tests for large n. Computed exactly with modular arithmetic.

name: Wilson Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when p is a Wilson prime, i.e. (p − 1)! ≡ −1 modulo p², not just modulo p.
notes: Only three Wilson primes are known: 5, 13 and 563.

name: Wieferich Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when p is prime and 2^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p²).
notes: Only 1093 and 3511 are known; they arose in work on Fermat's Last Theorem.

name: Fermat Probable-Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when a^(n−1) ≡ 1 (mod n). Every prime passes; a composite that passes is a Fermat pseudoprime to base a.
notes: 341 = 11 × 31 passes for base 2, so the test alone cannot prove primality.

name: Fermat Pseudoprime Test
description: Returns 1 when n is composite yet satisfies a^(n−1) ≡ 1 (mod n): a Fermat pseudoprime to base a.
notes: The smallest base-2 pseudoprime is 341; 561 is also a Carmichael number.

name: Carmichael Number Test (Korselt)
description: Returns 1 when n is a Carmichael number: composite, and λ(n) divides n − 1, so every base coprime to n fools the Fermat test.
notes: Korselt's criterion (squarefree with p − 1 | n − 1 for each prime p) is equivalent. The first ones are 561, 1105, 1729.

name: Euler–Jacobi Pseudoprime Test
expression: if(mod(n, 2) == 0, 0, (1 - isprime(n)) * (mod(powmod(a, (n - 1) / 2, n) - jacobi(a, n), n) == 0))
description: Returns 1 when the odd composite n satisfies Euler's criterion a^((n−1)/2) ≡ (a/n) (mod n) with the Jacobi symbol — an Euler–Jacobi pseudoprime.
notes: This is the check used by the Solovay–Strassen test; it catches most Carmichael numbers. 561 passes for base 2.

name: Primorial n#
description: Multiplies all primes up to n (the primorial n#).
notes: 20# = 2·3·5·7·11·13·17·19 = 9,699,690. Exact while the product stays below 2^53.

name: Primorial Prime Test (p# ± 1)
description: Returns 1 when p# + s is prime, where p# is the product of the primes up to p and s is +1 or −1.
notes: 11# + 1 = 2311 is prime; Euclid's proof of infinitely many primes uses numbers of this form.

name: Factorial Prime Test (n! ± 1)
description: Returns 1 when n! + s is prime (s = +1 or −1).
notes: 11! + 1 = 39,916,801 is prime. Exact for n up to 18.

name: Sum of Primes up to n
description: Adds every prime less than or equal to n.
notes: The primes up to 100 sum to 1060. Counts up to n one by one, so keep n at or below a million.

name: Sum of Reciprocals of Primes
description: Adds 1/p over the primes p ≤ x. The sum grows without bound, but only like ln ln x (Mertens' second theorem).
notes: Euler showed the full series diverges, which gives another proof that there are infinitely many primes.

name: Mertens' Second Theorem Estimate
description: Estimates the sum of 1/p over primes p ≤ x as ln ln x + M, where M ≈ 0.261497 is the Meissel–Mertens constant.
notes: The error tends to zero as x grows; compare with the exact sum of reciprocals of primes.

name: Mertens' Third Theorem Estimate
description: Estimates the product of (1 − 1/p) over primes p ≤ x as e^(−γ)/ln x, where γ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant.
notes: This is the proportion of integers with no prime factor up to x, roughly speaking.

name: Product of (1 − 1/p) over Primes
description: Multiplies (1 − 1/p) over every prime p ≤ x — the exact value that Mertens' third theorem approximates.
notes: For x = 1000 the product is about 0.0809; e^(−γ)/ln x gives about 0.0813.

name: Chebyshev Function θ(x)
description: Chebyshev's first function θ(x): the sum of ln p over primes p ≤ x, equal to the logarithm of the primorial.
notes: The prime number theorem is equivalent to θ(x) ~ x.

name: Chebyshev Function ψ(x)
description: Chebyshev's second function ψ(x): the sum of the von Mangoldt function Λ(n) for n ≤ x, i.e. ln p for every prime power p^k ≤ x.
notes: Equal to the logarithm of lcm(1, 2, …, x). The prime number theorem is equivalent to ψ(x) ~ x.

name: Von Mangoldt Function Λ(n)
description: Gives ln p when n is a power of a prime p, and 0 otherwise.
notes: Λ(81) = ln 3 because 81 = 3^4. It is the weight in Chebyshev's ψ function and in the explicit formula for primes.

name: Least Common Multiple of 1…n
description: Gives the smallest number divisible by every integer from 1 to n.
notes: lcm(1, …, 20) = 232,792,560. Its logarithm is Chebyshev's ψ(n).

name: Logarithmic Integral li(x)
description: Computes the logarithmic integral li(x), the integral of 1/ln t from 0 to x (principal value), the best simple estimate of π(x).

name: Offset Logarithmic Integral Li(x)
description: Computes the offset logarithmic integral Li(x) = li(x) − li(2), the integral of 1/ln t from 2 to x.
notes: Avoids the singularity at t = 1 and is the form used in many prime-counting bounds.

name: Riemann Prime-Counting Function R(x)
description: Riemann's R(x) = Σ μ(k)/k · li(x^(1/k)), a sharper estimate of π(x) than li(x), computed with the fast-converging Gram series 1 + Σ (ln x)^k / (k · k! · ζ(k+1)).
notes: The first 100 terms of the Gram series are used, plenty for x up to 10^15. R(10^6) ≈ 78,527.4 against π(10^6) = 78,498.

name: Prime Number Theorem Error li(x) − π(x)
description: Measures how far li(x) overestimates the number of primes up to x.
notes: The difference is positive for every x checked so far, yet Littlewood proved it changes sign infinitely often (first somewhere below about 10^316).

name: Legendre's Prime-Counting Estimate
description: Estimates π(x) with Legendre's empirical formula x/(ln x − 1.08366), proposed in 1808.
notes: Accurate for moderate x but asymptotically no better than x/(ln x − 1).

name: Prime-Counting Estimate x/(ln x − 1)
description: Estimates π(x) by x/(ln x − 1), the second-order improvement on x/ln x from the prime number theorem.
notes: Asymptotically the best choice of constant in x/(ln x − A) is A = 1.

name: Dusart Bounds for π(x) (Lower)
description: A proven lower bound for π(x) (Dusart 1998), valid for x ≥ 599.
notes: At x = 10^6 it gives about 78,030, just below π(10^6) = 78,498.

name: Dusart Bounds for π(x) (Upper)
description: A proven upper bound for π(x) (Dusart 1998), valid for x > 1.
notes: At x = 10^6 it gives about 78,543, just above π(10^6) = 78,498.

name: Rosser Lower Bound for the n-th Prime
description: A proven lower bound for the n-th prime p_n (Dusart 1999, sharpening Rosser), valid for n ≥ 2.
notes: For n = 10,000 it gives about 104,306, below p_n = 104,729.

name: Cipolla Estimate of the n-th Prime
description: Estimates the n-th prime with the first three terms of Cipolla's asymptotic expansion.
notes: For n = 10,000 it gives about 104,392 against the true 104,729.

name: Average Prime Gap near x
description: By the prime number theorem the average gap between consecutive primes near x is about ln x.
notes: Near one million primes are on average about 13.8 apart.

name: Cramér's Conjecture Gap Bound
description: Cramér conjectured that the gap after a prime p is O((ln p)²); this gives that scale.
notes: All known maximal gaps are below (ln p)², though the conjecture is unproved.

name: Bertrand's Postulate Check
description: Returns 1 when there is a prime between n and 2n, as Bertrand's postulate (Chebyshev's theorem) guarantees for every n > 1.
notes: A quick illustration of the theorem; the result is always 1 for n ≥ 2.

name: Goldbach Partition Count
description: Counts the ways to write an even number n as a sum of two primes p + q with p ≤ q.
notes: Goldbach's conjecture says the count is at least 1 for every even n > 2. 100 has 6 partitions (3+97, 11+89, 17+83, 29+71, 41+59, 47+53).

name: Twin Prime Pairs up to x
description: Counts the twin-prime pairs (p, p + 2) with p + 2 ≤ x.
notes: There are 35 pairs up to 1000.

name: Hardy–Littlewood Twin Prime Estimate
description: Estimates the number of twin-prime pairs up to x as 2C₂ ∫₂ˣ dt/(ln t)², with the twin prime constant C₂ ≈ 0.660162.
notes: Conjectural but very accurate: about 8,248 for x = 10^6 against the true 8,169.

name: Probability that n is Prime (PNT)
description: The prime number theorem's heuristic chance that a random integer near n is prime.
notes: Near one million about 1 number in 14 is prime.

name: Squarefree Test
description: Returns 1 when no square greater than 1 divides n (n is squarefree), using |μ(n)|.
notes: About 6/π² ≈ 60.8 % of integers are squarefree.

name: Semiprime Test
description: Returns 1 when n is the product of exactly two primes (not necessarily distinct).
notes: 221 = 13 × 17. RSA moduli are large semiprimes.

name: Sphenic Number Test
description: Returns 1 when n is the product of three distinct primes.
notes: The smallest is 30 = 2 × 3 × 5. A sphenic number has exactly 8 divisors.

name: k-Almost Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when n has exactly k prime factors counted with multiplicity (a k-almost prime).
notes: 72 = 2³ × 3² is a 5-almost prime. Primes are the 1-almost primes.

name: Smooth Number Test
description: Returns 1 when every prime factor of n is at most B (n is B-smooth).
notes: 5-smooth numbers are the "regular" or Hamming numbers; smooth numbers drive factoring algorithms such as the quadratic sieve.

name: Rough Number Test
description: Returns 1 when every prime factor of n is at least k (n is k-rough).
notes: 221 = 13 × 17 is 11-rough. Rough numbers are what remains after sieving out small primes.

name: Powerful Number Test
description: Returns 1 when p² divides n for every prime p dividing n (n is powerful, or squarefull).
notes: 72 = 2³ × 3² is powerful; 12 = 2² × 3 is not.

name: Radical of n (Squarefree Kernel)
description: Multiplies the distinct prime factors of n, giving the largest squarefree divisor rad(n).
notes: rad(720) = 2 × 3 × 5 = 30. The radical is central to the abc conjecture.

name: abc Triple Quality
description: Computes the quality q = ln c / ln rad(abc) of a coprime triple a + b = c. The abc conjecture says q > 1 + ε happens only finitely often.
notes: The default 2 + 3^10·109 = 23^5 has the highest known quality, about 1.6299 (Reyssat).

name: Smallest Prime Factor
description: Gives the smallest prime dividing n.
notes: 1001 = 7 × 11 × 13, so the answer is 7. For a prime n it is n itself.

name: Largest Prime Factor
description: Gives the largest prime dividing n.
notes: The largest prime factor of 600,851,475,143 is 6857 (Project Euler problem 3).

name: Number of Distinct Prime Factors ω(n)
description: Counts the different primes dividing n.

name: Number of Prime Factors Ω(n)
description: Counts the prime factors of n with multiplicity.

name: Hardy–Ramanujan Typical Number of Prime Factors
description: Hardy and Ramanujan showed that a typical integer near n has about ln ln n distinct prime factors.
notes: Even near 10^9 a typical number has only about 3 distinct prime factors; the Erdős–Kac theorem adds a normal spread of √(ln ln n).

name: Erdős–Kac Standardised Score
description: Standardises the number of distinct prime factors of n. By the Erdős–Kac theorem this score is approximately standard normal over integers near n.
notes: 9,699,690 = 20# has 8 distinct primes, far above the typical ≈ 2.8, a score near 3.

name: Proth's Theorem Test
description: For a Proth number n = k·2^m + 1 with k < 2^m, returns 1 when a^((n−1)/2) ≡ −1 (mod n), which proves n prime (Proth's theorem).
notes: 97 = 3·2⁵ + 1 is proved prime with a = 5. A result of 0 with a quadratic non-residue a proves n composite.

name: Pépin's Test for Fermat Numbers
description: Returns 1 when the Fermat number F_n = 2^(2^n) + 1 is prime, using Pépin's test 3^((F_n − 1)/2) ≡ −1 (mod F_n).
notes: F₀ to F₄ (3, 5, 17, 257, 65537) are prime; F₅ = 4,294,967,297 = 641 × 6,700,417 is not. Exact for n up to 5.

name: Form of Fermat Number Factors (Euler–Lucas)
description: Every prime factor of the Fermat number F_n (n ≥ 2) has the form k·2^(n+2) + 1; this lists the candidates.
notes: k = 5, n = 5 gives 641, the factor of F₅ that Euler found in 1732.

name: Primes between n and 2n
description: Counts the primes p with n < p ≤ 2n. Bertrand's postulate says there is at least one; the count grows like n/ln n.
notes: There are 135 primes between 1000 and 2000.

name: Primes in an Interval [a, b]
description: Counts the primes between a and b inclusive.
notes: There are 75 primes between 1,000,000 and 1,001,000, close to the expected 1000/ln(10⁶) ≈ 72.

name: Number of d-Digit Primes
description: Counts the primes with exactly d decimal digits.
notes: There are 68,906 six-digit primes. Exact up to d = 11.

name: Chance a Random d-Digit Number Is Prime
description: Gives the exact share of d-digit numbers that are prime.
notes: About 7.66 % of six-digit numbers are prime, close to 1/ln(500,000) ≈ 7.6 %.

name: Landau's Problem: Primes of the Form n² + 1
description: Counts the primes n² + 1 up to x. Whether there are infinitely many is one of Landau's four unsolved problems (1912).
notes: There are 19 such primes up to 10,000 (2, 5, 17, 37, 101, …).

name: Legendre's Conjecture Check
description: Returns 1 when there is a prime between n² and (n + 1)². Legendre conjectured this for every n ≥ 1; it is still unproved.
notes: Between 100² and 101² lies 10,007.

name: Andrica's Conjecture Gap √p(n+1) − √p(n)
description: Computes √p₍ₙ₊₁₎ − √pₙ. Andrica conjectured it is always below 1; the largest known value, at n = 4 (7 and 11), is about 0.6708.
notes: The conjecture would imply a prime between n² and (n + 1)² (Legendre).

name: Sum of the First n Primes
description: Adds the first n primes.
notes: The first 100 primes sum to 24,133; the sum grows like (n² ln n)/2.

name: Euler's Prime-Generating Polynomial n² + n + 41
description: Evaluates Euler's polynomial n² + n + 41, which is prime for every n from 0 to 39.
notes: n = 39 gives 1601 (prime); n = 40 gives 1681 = 41².

name: Primes Produced by n² + n + 41
description: Counts how many of the values n² + n + 41 for n = 0 … m are prime.
notes: For n up to 99, 86 of the 100 values are prime — far more than for a random polynomial of that size.

name: Isolated Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when p is prime but neither p − 2 nor p + 2 is (a prime that is not part of any twin pair).
notes: 23 is isolated: 21 and 25 are composite.

name: Prime Power Test
description: Returns 1 when n = p^k for a prime p and k ≥ 1.
notes: 243 = 3⁵. Finite fields exist exactly for prime-power sizes.

name: Fortunate Number
expression: nextprime(prod(k, 2, p, if(isprime(k), k, 1)) + 1) - prod(k, 2, p, if(isprime(k), k, 1))
description: Gives the smallest m > 1 for which p# + m is prime, where p# is the primorial. Fortune conjectured it is always prime.
notes: For p = 11 (11# = 2310) the Fortunate number is 23.

name: Pierpont Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when n is a prime of the form 2^u·3^v + 1 (a Pierpont prime).
notes: Regular polygons with a Pierpont-prime number of sides can be constructed with an angle trisector. 97 = 2⁵·3 + 1.

name: Circular Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when every cyclic rotation of the digits of n is prime.
notes: 197, 971 and 719 are all prime. There are only 13 circular primes below 10^6.

name: Left-Truncatable Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when n stays prime as its leading digits are removed one at a time.
notes: 9137, 137, 37, 7 are all prime. The largest such prime (without zeros) has 24 digits.

name: Right-Truncatable Prime Test
description: Returns 1 when n stays prime as its last digits are removed one at a time.
notes: 7393, 739, 73, 7 are all prime. There are exactly 83 right-truncatable primes; the largest is 73,939,133.

name: Digits of a Mersenne Number 2^p − 1
description: Counts the decimal digits of 2^p − 1.
notes: The Mersenne prime 2^136,279,841 − 1 found in 2024 has 41,024,320 digits.

name: Twin Prime Constant (Partial Product)
description: Multiplies p(p − 2)/(p − 1)² over odd primes p ≤ x, approaching the twin prime constant C₂ ≈ 0.6601618.
notes: C₂ appears in the Hardy–Littlewood estimate of how many twin primes there are.

name: Artin's Constant (Partial Product)
description: Multiplies 1 − 1/(p(p − 1)) over primes p ≤ x, approaching Artin's constant ≈ 0.3739558.
notes: Artin conjectured this is the share of primes for which 2 (or any suitable a) is a primitive root.

name: Share of Primes with 2 as a Primitive Root
description: Finds the fraction of odd primes up to x for which 2 is a primitive root, to compare with Artin's constant 0.3739.
notes: Up to 10,000 the share is about 0.3795.

name: Mertens' First Theorem Remainder
expression: sum(p, 2, x, isprime(p) * ln(p) / p) - ln(x)
description: Computes Σ_{p ≤ x} (ln p)/p − ln x. Mertens proved it stays bounded; it tends to about −1.3325.
notes: Up to 10,000 the value is about −1.3163.

name: Meissel–Mertens Constant Estimate
description: Estimates the Meissel–Mertens constant M ≈ 0.2614972 as Σ_{p ≤ x} 1/p − ln ln x.
notes: The difference shrinks slowly, like 1/ln x.
